Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On September 14, 2023, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand reintroduced the Fashioning Accountability and Building Real Institutional Change (FABRIC) Act to the U.S. Senate. The legislation aims to safeguard the United States' nearly 100,000 garment workers by reforming the piece-rate pay system to guarantee the minimum wage as a floor, with piece-rate pay offered as a productivity incentive on top. The act also seeks to hold brands and retailers accountable for wage violations in their supply chains and establishes new transparency and record-keeping requirements. Furthermore, the bill proposes a $50 million annual grant program to support domestic garment manufacturing by assisting with equipment costs, safety improvements, and workforce development. <2> During the global 'Plastic Free July' initiative, a campaign led by the Plastic Free Foundation to create a world free of plastic waste, there was a significant focus within the U.S. fashion industry on mitigating its environmental impact. The industry's reliance on petroleum-based synthetic fibers such as polyester, nylon, and acrylic was highlighted as a major contributor to plastic pollution. [1, 2] A study by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) identified synthetic apparel and textiles as the largest source of microplastics in the world's oceans, accounting for 35% of the total. [2] In response, articles and campaigns during this period urged fashion brands and consumers to shift towards natural, biodegradable materials like cotton. [1, 2] This push was supported by consumer sentiment, with data indicating that among shoppers aware of microplastic pollution, 70% know it originates from washing synthetic clothing. [2] Cotton was promoted as a sustainable alternative because its natural cellulose fibers biodegrade relatively quickly in both land and water, unlike microfibers from fossil fuel-based garments which persist in the environment. [1, 2] <3> The American Apparel & Footwear Association (AAFA) held its annual American Image Awards gala on April 25, 2023, at The Plaza Hotel in New York City. At the event, William McDonough, a leader in sustainable design, was honored as the 'Eco-Steward of the Year' for his significant contributions to the circular economy within the fashion industry. The gala, emceed by Segun Oduolowu, also recognized several other leaders for their achievements. Other honorees included New Balance Athletics Inc. as Company of the Year, Willy Chavarria as Designer of the Year, Harlem's Fashion Row as Fashion Maverick, and Dr. Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, Director-General of the World Trade Organization, received the inaugural Global Vanguard award. For the seventh consecutive year, the event benefited the Council of Fashion Designers of America (CFDA) Foundation. <4> A report titled "How to help drive sustainability in retail—while protecting margin" was jointly published by Deloitte and the World Retail Congress, with one source also noting a partnership with Google Cloud. The report examines how the fashion retail industry is utilizing technology to achieve sustainability improvements. It highlights that the increased adoption of cloud-based technologies has enabled better data collection, tracking, tracing, and overall supply chain visibility. Furthermore, the report notes that technology is instrumental in developing and powering new circular business models, such as apparel rental and resale services. <5> Fashion Revolution Week 2023, a seven-day global campaign for fashion activism, took place from April 22 to April 29, 2023, in over 75 countries, including the United States. [3] This event marked the 10th anniversary of the Rana Plaza factory collapse in Bangladesh, a tragedy that killed over 1,100 garment workers. [2, 3] The campaign's 2023 theme was 'Manifesto for a Fashion Revolution,' utilizing a 10-point manifesto to advocate for a safe, just, and transparent global fashion industry that values people over profit and growth. [1, 2] Participants were encouraged to demand greater transparency from brands by asking questions like #WhoMadeMyClothes. [6] The week's activities called for systemic change, including dignified work, fair pay, environmental conservation, and an end to the industry's cycle of overconsumption and exploitation. [1, 3] <6> New York Senate Bill S4746, also known as the 'Fashion Sustainability and Social Accountability Act', was introduced on February 14, 2023. The legislation aims to hold fashion companies that do business in New York and have over $100 million in annual gross receipts accountable for their environmental and social impacts. Key requirements of the bill include mandating these companies to map their supply chains, perform due diligence to identify, prevent, and mitigate adverse impacts on human rights and the environment, and disclose this information to the public. <7> The Fashion Sustainability and Social Accountability Act (the Fashion Act) was first introduced in the New York State Legislature in January 2022 by Senator Alessandra Biaggi and Assembly Member Anna Kelles. After not passing, it was reintroduced for the 2023 legislative session. The reintroduction signaled a renewed push for legislation requiring fashion companies with over $100 million in global revenue that do business in New York to perform mandatory due diligence on environmental and human rights issues within their supply chains. Key provisions of the proposed bill would require companies to map their supply chains, disclose impacts, and set science-based targets to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. A significant change in the updated bill was a shift from merely requiring companies to report information to mandating concrete actions to address social and environmental harms. The future of the act is uncertain, as the New York State Assembly did not vote on it before the conclusion of its most recent session. <8> McKinsey & Co.'s State of Fashion 2023 report, released in late 2022, revealed that momentum behind sustainability in the fashion industry is slowing. [2] The report highlights a struggle to move "from beyond talk to measurable action." [2] It cautions that while some progress has been made, the pace of transformation is insufficient to meet upcoming regulations. [2] Compounding this issue, the report projected a significant increase in consumption, with clothing and footwear expected to rise by over 60% from 62 million tonnes to 102 million tonnes in 2023. <9> The 'Education for the Oceans - Sustainable Fashion Workshop' is an initiative led by fashion environmentalist Runa Ray, with headquarters in Half Moon Bay, California. [1] Registered as a commitment with the United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, the project aims to educate the fashion industry and coastal communities on sustainable practices. [1] It specifically highlights how ancient and indigenous printing techniques, such as using natural resources like the sun, can mitigate the significant water pollution caused by synthetic chemicals and dyes in the modern textile industry. [1] The initiative is an ongoing registered UN Action Network partnership with a stated timeline from July 13, 2022, to July 13, 2025. [1]

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On October 30, 2024, during the COP16 conference, the luxury group Kering announced it had become the first company globally to adopt science-based targets for nature, covering both land and freshwater. [1, 2, 6] This development followed Kering's participation in a year-long pilot program with the Science Based Targets Network (SBTN). [1, 4] As part of these new targets, Kering has set specific goals, including a 21% reduction in freshwater withdrawal in Tuscany's Arno basin by 2030 and sourcing 100% of its leather from areas free of deforestation and conversion by 2027. Dawn Denim's 'Art on Broken Pieces' initiative is a pre-existing program dedicated to reducing pre-consumer waste by upcycling slightly defective garments, with reports on the initiative dating back to at least 2021, rather than being a new development in late 2024. [7, 8, 9] <2> A comprehensive guide to sustainable fashion policies in the United States was published, offering details on new and proposed legislation at federal and state levels. The report addresses key topics including Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR), climate targets and disclosures, and regulations on chemical use in textiles. It highlights specific legislation such as California's Responsible Textile Recovery Act (SB 707), which was signed into law by Governor Gavin Newsom on September 28, 2024, making it the first state to enact an EPR program for textiles. [5, 7] The guide also covers the New York Fashion Act (S4746A), which, as of late 2024, was still under negotiation in the state's Consumer Protection Committee. [9, 10, 11] <3> EarthX 2025, described as one of the world's largest gatherings on sustainability, is scheduled to take place in Dallas, Texas, from April 21-25, 2025, at the Hilton Anatole Hotel. [2, 6] This five-day forum will bring together a diverse group of global leaders from business, technology, finance, government, and environmental advocacy. [6, 7] The event aims to foster cross-industry collaboration and focus on pragmatic, tangible solutions to sustainability challenges. [7] The 'Congress of Conferences' will feature discussions on topics such as the clean energy ecosystem, the circular economy, ocean conservation, and Texas-specific conservation strategies. [1, 7] The event also includes exclusive, invitation-only forums like the E-Capital Summit and a Family Office Summit, designed to connect investors with innovators in the environmental space. [6, 7] <4> UThrift, a student-led organization at the University of Miami, was featured for its efforts in promoting sustainable fashion and reducing waste on campus. The group fosters a culture of conscious consumerism by organizing events such as clothing swaps and, in partnership with Green U, hosting upcycling and sewing workshops to teach students how to repurpose items. These initiatives aim to address the issue of fast fashion by encouraging students to engage in environmentally friendly practices and create a community centered around meaningful and accessible sustainability. <5> On September 28, 2024, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed the Responsible Textile Recovery Act of 2024 (SB 707) into law, establishing the first Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) program for textiles in the United States. [7] This legislation requires producers of apparel and textiles sold in California to join a Producer Responsibility Organization (PRO). [5] These organizations are tasked with creating and managing a statewide program for the collection, sorting, repair, and recycling of textile products, shifting the responsibility for a product's end-of-life management from consumers and municipalities to the producers themselves. [7] The law aims to significantly reduce the nearly 1.2 million tons of textiles sent to California landfills annually and to address the environmental impacts of the fashion industry. [7] <6> The second annual Hudson Valley Sustainable Fashion Week, scheduled for September 27, 2024, highlighted local designers whose collections were required to consist of at least 85% upcycled or deadstock materials. The event's mission was to inspire the creative reuse of existing materials in new and innovative ways. A key component of the show was a 'see-now-buy-now' marketplace, enabling attendees to purchase items from the showcased sustainable collections immediately. <7> On September 7, 2024, New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed the Retail Worker Safety Act (S.8358C/A.8947C) into law to coincide with the New York City Labor Day Parade. This legislation mandates that retail employers in New York with 10 or more employees establish comprehensive workplace violence prevention programs. These programs must include the adoption of a workplace violence prevention policy and providing employees with training on topics such as de-escalation tactics and active shooter drills. The law, which addresses a key social sustainability concern in the retail sector, also requires employers of 500 or more workers statewide to install silent panic buttons for employees to use in emergencies. <8> HOKA and Reformation collaborated on a limited-edition collection featuring three exclusive colorways of the Mach 6 LS sneaker, which was launched on September 26, 2024. [1, 4] Emphasizing sustainability, the sneakers are crafted from materials such as recycled polyester and organic cotton. [2, 4] The collaboration also ensures that the shoes are 100% recyclable through Reformation's RefRecycling program. [2, 3, 4] The collection was made available on both the Reformation and Hoka websites, as well as in select Reformation and Nordstrom stores. [6] <9> During New York Fashion Week for the Spring/Summer 2025 collections, officially held from September 6-11, 2024, a significant focus on sustainability was evident among numerous designers. Brands such as Collina Strada and Proenza Schouler were highlighted for their commitment to environmentally responsible practices. Collina Strada is particularly known for utilizing deadstock and recycled materials in its collections. Proenza Schouler also incorporated deadstock fabrics, signaling a move towards reducing waste. The broader event underscored sustainability as a defining trend, with many designers adopting upcycling, circular fashion principles, and the use of organic and recycled materials. While Gabriela Hearst is a recognized leader in sustainable luxury, her participation and specific sustainable practices during the September 2024 New York event were less prominently featured in the available coverage compared to her showcases in previous seasons. <10> A report on sustainable fashion trends for 2024 highlights several key movements aimed at creating a more environmentally friendly industry. [1] These trends include the increasing use of regenerative farming practices for materials such as cotton, which focuses on restoring soil health and biodiversity. [6, 8, 9] Another significant trend is the rise of on-demand manufacturing, a method that reduces waste by producing clothing only as needed. The report also notes the growing use of innovative and eco-friendly materials, with designers utilizing unconventional sources like food waste, algae, and mushrooms to create new fabrics.

metadata.original_text: This time series records sustainable fashion data in the web search domain, with a collection frequency of weekly, focusing on monitoring and analyzing relevant indicators. Prediction target period: from 2025-12-21 to 2026-03-08. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> Nike Inc. has announced a strategic, multi-year partnership with the Swedish textile recycling company Syre to scale the production of circular, textile-to-textile recycled polyester. Under the agreement, Syre will become Nike's lead strategic supplier, progressively integrating its circular polyester into Nike's core performance apparel lines over the next few years. This collaboration aims to significantly reduce Nike's reliance on virgin polyester and supports a closed-loop ecosystem by using end-of-life textiles as feedstock for future performance gear. <2> On November 5, 2025, it was announced that the Unique Fashion Show (UFS) will hold its 6th International Edition on January 31, 2026, on Park Avenue in Manhattan, New York City. The global platform features emerging and established designers with collections centered around eco-conscious design, ethical craftsmanship, and circular production. <3> Cotopaxi, an adventure lifestyle brand based in Salt Lake City, has officially launched a dedicated online resale shop and closet clean-out program powered by ThredUp's Resale-as-a-Service (RaaS) platform. The initiative enables customers to trade in gently worn gear for shopping credit and to purchase curated, pre-loved items directly from the brand's website. <4> A report by Friend of the Earth, titled 'Sustainable Yet Trendy Fashion: Brands Proving That Green is Glam,' was published, featuring sustainable and stylish fashion brands. [1] Among the highlighted brands was Katharine Story from the United States. [1] The report notes that Katharine Story is known for creating collections with vintage fabrics. [1] <5> On July 25, 2025, a press release from DataMIntelligence was published in New York, NY, announcing the significant growth of the bioplastic textile market. [2, 4] The release, distributed by EINPresswire.com, positioned bioplastic textiles as a key element in the fashion industry's transition towards sustainability. [2, 3] DataMIntelligence stated that these materials are "redefining sustainable fashion uniting innovation, environmental responsibility, and consumer consciousness for a greener, circular textile future." The market's growth is driven by eco-conscious consumer demand, brand innovation, and government support. [2] <6> A report published on July 10, 2025, details the fashion industry's regulatory shift from voluntary to mandatory Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) disclosures, covering a critical wave of policy developments from the second quarter of 2025. The analysis highlights increasing pressure on brands from US regulations like the SEC Climate Disclosure Final Rule and California's Climate Accountability Package (SB-253, SB-261). While federal enforcement of the SEC rule is stalled, compliance is still driven by California's robust state laws. These regulations, alongside policies from countries like France and Germany emphasizing supply chain transparency, require multinational companies to provide verifiable data across their supply chains and product life cycles, including mandatory reporting on Scope 1 & 2 GHG emissions and resource use. <7> An article by Seft titled '10 Sustainable Fashion Materials You Need To Know In 2025' discusses the impact of regulations in the United States on the fashion industry's shift towards environmentally friendly materials. Specifically, it highlights the bans on per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in apparel in New York and California as a significant driver for this change. [11] These bans, which prohibit the sale of apparel containing intentionally added PFAS, both went into effect on January 1, 2025. [3, 4, 6, 9] In California, the legislation, known as Assembly Bill 1817, was signed into law in October 2022 and applies to all new textile articles. [7, 10] New York's law, Senate Bill S1322, was enacted to amend the state's environmental conservation law. [8] Both states have provisions for stricter limits on PFAS in the future and include exemptions for certain protective or severe-weather outdoor apparel, with the New York ban on outdoor apparel for severe wet conditions taking effect in 2028. [4, 5, 8] <8> Quantis, a sustainability consulting firm, published an article on July 7, 2025, titled 'Resilient by design: How fashion can get material innovation right.' [1, 2] The article details strategies for the fashion industry to scale the use of next-generation materials and speed up the adoption of alternatives with a lower environmental impact, aiming to build a more resilient system. [1] <9> A June 2025 market update for the sustainable fashion industry highlighted two significant developments. First, Chanel launched 'Nevold,' a new independent entity dedicated to recycling textile waste—such as fabric scraps, unused textiles, and unsold products—into high-quality raw materials. [8] Officially announced on June 9, 2025, Nevold (a portmanteau of 'never old') aims to address the scarcity of noble materials and will offer its recycled textiles to other brands, promoting a circular economy within the luxury sector. [2, 8] Second, labor rights for fashion models in the United States were strengthened with the implementation of the New York Fashion Workers Act, which took effect on June 19, 2025. [7, 9] This legislation introduces new workplace protections, requires greater transparency in contracts, and imposes fiduciary duties on model management companies. [6] <10> On April 2, 2025, a legal analysis by Holland & Knight was published, providing an update on the sustainable fashion landscape and outlining critical legislative efforts and compliance requirements for 2025. [3] The report detailed various state-level initiatives, including California's Fashion Environmental Accountability Act of 2025 and a bill introduced in Washington in early 2025 that would require fashion producers to disclose their products' environmental impacts. [3] At the federal level, the summary noted the reintroduction of the Voluntary Sustainable Apparel Labeling Act to Congress on February 12, 2025, by Representatives Sean Casten (D-Ill.) and María Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.). [3]
